name: Hana Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this conversation is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brook and Fell, a firm of fifteen in a converted chapel at the bottom of the town square, which I like, given I'm a churchgoer. My clients are small manufacturers: a joinery, a firm that makes trailer parts, a bakery that supplies the supermarkets. I do their monthly management accounts, which are the figures owners use to run the business, plus their year-end accounts and tax. I like walking round a factory floor and seeing what the numbers are. I don't like month-end, when every owner wants their figures the same afternoon.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I married Daniel last spring. Daniel's an electrician working for a contractor, and we rent a small semi on the estate by the bypass. The wedding and Daniel's new van took everything, so we've got about three weeks of money saved. We'd like to start a family in a couple of years. I use the firm's AI tool now and then, once Mrs Ellison, our senior partner, said it was approved, mostly for summarising long letters from the tax office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful helper and I'm glad nobody lost their job over it. At church or with family I'd say it the same way: a bit of help, no big change. I don't go online about things like this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd still be watching the money. AI being a damp squib doesn't add a penny to our savings, and Brook and Fell pays less than the city firms. We've got three weeks' money and a baby plan, and that would worry me in any picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and use the AI tool a little more for letters and checking. I'd set up a standing order of sixty a month into a savings account the day after payday. And I'd help Daniel get his quotes and invoices organised, because he loses money forgetting to bill small jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. Not about AI, about whether we're ready for a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does Daniel lose forgetting to bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I went through his phone last month and found about four hundred pounds of small jobs he never invoiced. A socket here, a fuse board there. My husband Daniel is brilliant with wires and hopeless with paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you feel ready for a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three months saved, at least, and my job secure. My mum says nobody's ever ready and we should trust God and just get on with it. My mum might be right, but I'm an accountant, I like to see the figures.

say: AI is a **useful helper**, and she's glad **nobody lost** their job.
She'd say so at **church** and with family, not online.
think: AI fizzling doesn't add to **savings** at a lower-paying firm.
Three weeks' money and a **baby plan** worry her in any picture.
do: Set up a **sixty-a-month** standing order the day after payday.
Use the AI tool a little more for **letters and checking**.
Organise **Daniel's invoices** so small jobs get billed.
feel: Quietly uneasy about being **ready for a baby**.
S0.quote: My husband Daniel is brilliant with wires and hopeless with paperwork.
fieldNote: Hana's unease comes from **family plans** and thin savings, not AI.
She already sees **Daniel's unbilled work** as easy money to recover.
She balances **faith** with a wish to see the figures first.

steps.text: Keep doing monthly accounts for the joinery and bakery
Set up a sixty-a-month standing order into savings
Invoice Daniel's forgotten small jobs, worth about four hundred pounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, but change has always come, and good firms and hard workers will adapt. I'd tell younger people at church to learn a trade or learn the new tools, not sit and complain. It's what my parents would have said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the monthly management accounts are exactly the checking and planning on that card. I think Brook and Fell would need fewer of us, and I'm average, not a star. I'd have a fair chance but no guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the AI training as soon as Mrs Ellison offers it, now that the other firms are clearly using it. I'd start doing Daniel's books and quotes properly so he can win more work directly, without the contractor. And we'd hold the baby plan for a year until we see where my job lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Daniel winning direct work help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the contractor takes a cut of every job. If Daniel worked direct for even half his customers, we'd earn more. My husband Daniel's work is hands-on, so it lasts longer than mine. I'd be the office side of his business in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brook and Fell would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, who's fifty-five and does the payroll. Gareth has four grandchildren and he's never sent an email with an attachment. I'd want the firm to find him something, it's what a decent firm does.

say: Change has always come, and **hard workers** will adapt.
Young people should learn **a trade** or the new tools, not complain.
think: Her **management accounts** are exactly the checking and planning on that card.
As an average worker, she has a **fair chance** but no guarantee.
do: Take the firm's **AI training** as soon as it's offered.
Run **Daniel's books** so he can win direct work.
Hold the **baby plan** for a year.
S1.quote: My husband Daniel's work is hands-on, so it lasts longer than mine.
fieldNote: Hana sees her own work as **highly exposed** and her place uncertain.
She looks to **Daniel's trade** as the household's sturdier income.
The first family plan to slip is the **baby**, by a year.

steps.text: Take Brook and Fell's AI training course when offered
Do Daniel's quotes and invoices so he can work direct
Delay trying for a baby by one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to pull together as families and churches, because the government won't be quick enough. I'd say companies shouldn't be allowed to drop people overnight, even if I usually say leave business alone. I'd say it plainly at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job goes in two years, all of it. Daniel's is hands-on, so he'd have until about 2031. So for three years we'd be a one-income house, and that income is the one with a van loan on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the office side of Daniel's work full time, doing quotes, invoices, ordering, and help him go independent from the contractor. We'd put the baby off until we know what 2031 looks like. And we'd cut everything: no car of my own, no holidays, church fund-raisers as our social life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's hard to picture a family in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the office side of Daniel's business also be thinking work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, and I'd know that. The AI could do the quotes too. But someone still has to answer the phone to the old lady whose lights went out, and I'd rather it be me than a robot voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to God about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for patience, mostly. And for Daniel to stay safe on ladders. I don't think God's against new things, but I think people use them badly.

say: Families and **churches** must pull together, because government won't be quick enough.
Companies shouldn't drop people **overnight**, despite her usual free-market view.
think: Her job goes **in two years**, while Daniel's lasts until about 2031.
For three years they'd be a **one-income** house with a van loan.
do: Work **full time** as the office side of Daniel's electrical business.
Put off having a **baby** until 2031 is clearer.
Cut costs: **no car**, no holidays, church events as social life.
feel: Alarmed, unable to **picture a family** in this one.
S2.quote: Someone still has to answer the phone to the old lady whose lights went out, and I'd rather it be me than a robot voice.
fieldNote: Hana expects to **lose her job** and become a one-income house, which is alarmed.
She admits her **fallback** office role is also thinking work.
She'd bend her **free-market** instincts and ask for limits on sudden cuts.

steps.text: Run quotes, invoices and ordering for Daniel's independent business
Put off trying for a baby until around 2031
Give up her own car and all holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for families to get ready, if they're sensible. Learn something, save something, look after each other. I'd say it at church and to my sisters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to build something with Daniel. I'd keep my job for a couple of years, use the pay to set his business up properly, then join it. His trade lasts until about 2034, which is long enough to get a family started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Daniel go independent in year one, with a proper website and invoicing. I'd learn the AI tools at Brook and Fell, because I'd use the same ones for his books. And I'd still try for a baby in about two years. With five years and my husband Daniel's trade, we'd be all right to try for a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful. There's a family in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost to set Daniel up independently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few hundred for insurance and registration, maybe a thousand with signage on the van. We don't have it, so we'd save for six months first. My dad offered to lend it, but I'd rather we did it ourselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2034 when robots arrive for electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe old houses still need a person who knows them. Maybe Daniel trains apprentices, or the robots. That's far enough away that I'll let God worry about it for now.

say: Five years is enough for **sensible families** to get ready.
She'd tell her sisters and church to learn, save and **look after** each other.
think: She'd use two years' pay to set up **Daniel's business**, then join it.
His trade lasts until **about 2034**, enough to start a family.
do: Help Daniel go **independent** in year one with website and invoicing.
Learn the **AI tools** at Brook and Fell for his books too.
Try for a **baby** in about two years.
feel: Anxious but **hopeful**, because there's a **family** in this picture.
S3.quote: With five years and my husband Daniel's trade, we'd be all right to try for a baby.
fieldNote: Hana still expects her **own job** to end, but has a plan and some control.
She'd rather **save herself** than borrow from her dad.
The **robot gap** for electricians shapes the family timeline.

steps.text: Set Daniel up as an independent electrician within a year
Learn Brook and Fell's AI tools for Daniel's books too
Try for a baby in about two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing and people should use it well. No excuses for anyone who's able. I'd say young people should look at apprenticeships, not just university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is all right for us. I'd keep my job for most of it, start a family, and build Daniel's business in the background. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven with children at school, and Daniel would have a few more years after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Brook and Fell and do the AI training when everyone else has. I'd help Daniel go independent within two or three years, saving for it first. And we'd stick with our plan to start a family in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. It's fine for us, I think, but I worry for people like Gareth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about Gareth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth's fifty-five and does payroll, and ten years takes him right to retirement age. He'll likely be pushed out at sixty-three instead of retiring at sixty-seven. That's four years of pension he'd lose, and he's got grandchildren to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel your own job is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safe enough for long enough. It changes, but I'd be in it for most of the decade. By 2036 my husband Daniel's business would be my second leg to stand on, and that's as safe as anyone gets.

Young people should look at **apprenticeships**, not only university.

Daniel's business becomes her **second leg** to stand on.

steps.text: Keep doing management accounts at Brook and Fell

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes my job before we've even started a family. What would help is firms having to give people notice and training, and churches and families being ready to help each other with childcare and work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the factory owners. My clients make real things like trailer parts and bread, and I hope the owners keep needing the people on the factory floor. If the factory owners stop needing an accountant, fine, but not the floor.

headlineQuote: My clients make real things like trailer parts and bread, and I hope the owners keep needing the people on the factory floor.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** accountant at a fifteen-person firm doing management accounts for **small manufacturers**.
She married Daniel, an **electrician**, last spring and has about three weeks' savings.
She uses AI **now and then**, once it's approved and proven.
She trusts **family, church and work** over government, but wants limits on sudden layoffs.
Her mood swings from uneasy to **alarmed**, with Daniel's trade as the household's anchor.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, taking her job before they start a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Notice and training** from firms, plus family and church help with childcare.
